doc.title: Warren Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 17, 2018

title: Growing up in a musical Chicago household; Charlie Parker at the door
summary: His father, a saxophonist and teacher of Gene Ammons and Johnny Griffin, repaired horns for visiting players including Parker; his mother was a harpist.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: The performance part of it yes, and the ensemble parts of it and working that hard was, but like the rest of school there were other ambitions that I had. There were other tastes that I had that I couldn’t satisfy simply within that one type of music. You know I had grown up around Chicago jazz all my life. My father was a saxophone player and a teacher, had notable students among them: Gene Ammons and Johnny Griffin. And these were kinds of people that I was used to being around and growing up with.
Your father taught those two players?
Yeah. Those were two of the ones he taught.

I mean everybody, Charlie Parker came to Chicago and his horn needed fixing, so the first person he came to was my father. And we’re sitting there looking at Bird. And all he wanted was to have his horn fixed. But I mean all the saxophone players came there to get their instruments repaired.
You knew who Bird was then?
You knew who Bird was at that time.

Oh absolutely. Sure. Yeah. Yeah by the time I was ten — well first of all there were musicians coming in and out of the house all the time you know. It was like a musical center. Because literally all the saxophone players came and others came and hung out you know. My mother was a harpist and she taught the harp and performed. All of my uncles and aunts were involved in music on both sides of the family. So it was not unusual to just be associated with musicians. I had made up my mind by the time I was three I was going to be a musician. And you know my ambitions never varied.
And your parents were on your side with that.
Oh yeah. Yeah, I mean not just my parents, the whole family.
